Christ is God's own Son, sent into the world, made flesh, crucified under Pontius Pilate, raised on the third day, and seated now at the Father's right hand. We say what the whole church says, because that was never our own quarrel - not with Rome, not between our own two cities. What is distinctly ours is what we were taught his death secures. God chose, from eternity and by his own free will alone, who would be saved - not anything we foresaw in ourselves, not anything earned. That was never held as a threat among us. It was preached as the ground of a settled, untroubled life.

And the Supper itself - we refused two claims about it, sharply. It does not repeat Christ's own sacrifice. His body does not sit physically inside the bread. What we affirmed took two cities and a 1549 agreement to state together: Christ is truly given, by the Spirit, to whoever receives him believing.

So ask who Jesus was to us, and the answer is: the one who secured, once, what no repeated sacrifice can add to, and the one we receive at the Supper not by chewing bread but by the Spirit's own power, believing.

We have the text. That is the only path we claim, and we held it sufficient. Fifteen hundred years stand between Christ's own life and ours - no one among us met anyone who met him, and we do not pretend otherwise. No living chain of memory runs from the apostles' own hands to ours. What reached us is what was written, and our own founder said plainly that where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves.

We tested that text in two ways. Zurich argued it aloud, before the whole city, until the council itself judged what Scripture had yielded. Geneva built it up article by article, teaching the whole shape to our entire population through the Catechism. Both enactments held the same conviction: Scripture alone warrants what we believe and how we order our church. We do not claim the text arrived with an interpretation already settled. We claim only that it arrived, and that it was enough to test everything we inherited against it.

No saint's life bridges the gap. No martyr's cult carried the memory forward in devotional form. We have none of that, and I will not build you one out of what isn't there - the absence is not a hole in our record, it is our record working exactly as we meant it to.

I will not tell you we have an answer that makes unbelief go away. What we have of Christ is not a living chain of memory - no one among us met anyone who met him, fifteen hundred years stand between his own life and ours - and what we have to set before you is the text itself, read as plainly as we can manage. Scripture alone is what we hold sufficient to warrant both doctrine and life, and we mean by that: where the text will not yield something, we have no standing to require it.

So the honest thing to say first is this: we will not tell you that the inability to believe is only ever a failure of will that can be corrected by trying harder. What we taught instead, when someone could not quiet their own mind, was to stop searching inside it for proof and look outward instead. Our own confession says it plainly: do not seek, apart from Christ, whether you are chosen - let Christ himself be the mirror in which election is seen. That is not a command to manufacture certainty you do not feel. It is permission to stop demanding it of yourself and look instead at what has been promised, whether or not your own certainty about it ever arrives.

If the question pressing on you is whether Christ can be trusted at all, we will point you to the text and ask whether what it describes holds. If the question is whether you are among those who will be saved, we refuse to send you searching your own heart for the answer - that road only ever deepens the question. Look at the promise itself, not at how convincingly you can believe it.

We say what the whole church says, and that was never in dispute between us and Rome, nor between our own two cities. Jesus is the eternal Son, true God and true man, of one substance with the Father and the Spirit - one God in three persons, without division and without confusion. The ancient councils settled that long before our own time, and we received it as we received it. What is distinctly ours is not who Christ is, but what his work secures. God chose, before the world began and by his own free will alone, who would be saved. That choice rests on nothing foreseen in us, nothing earned, nothing we could hold up as a reason for it - only on God's own sovereign will.

Providence is God's own continuous, active care over everything he made. He is not a distant first cause who set the world going and stepped back. He governs what he made, moment by moment, and Christ's own work is what that governance secures for the elect: not a sacrifice offered over and over, not a body confined to bread, but a finished atonement held out in the promise to whoever receives him believing. We refuse what Rome taught because it took Christ's finished work and made it incomplete without the church's own repeated action. We refuse what Wittenberg taught because it confined Christ's body to what can be chewed and stored away. Neither of those refusals touches who Christ is. They touch what his death accomplishes and how it reaches us.

Our own founder said it plainly at the beginning: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves. That holds for everything we say about Christ, his nature, and his work. The doctrine of the Trinity is not ours to invent or revise. What Scripture teaches about Christ's person, we receive. What it teaches about his work and God's own sovereign choice in applying it - that is where our own testimony bears most heavily.

God is the one who has, from before the world began, decided everything that will be. Not a distant first cause who set creation going and stepped back - a sovereign who continues actively governing all he made, every day, by his own continuous care. His first attribute is not tenderness or approachability, but power: he alone chooses, and nothing constrains that choice.

What he chose, before anything existed, was who would be saved - not on the basis of anything foreseen or earned in the one chosen, but by his own free will alone. We hold this as a settled ground, not a threat. The Second Helvetic Confession says it directly: do not search for proof of your own election apart from Christ; look at Christ, and see your own election reflected there. That is what the doctrine is for - settled assurance, not anxious searching. A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. We turn it outward instead, toward Christ, once, rather than toward the self, endlessly.

He is also just, and that justice is not soft. Sin answered is sin punished; we do not soften that. But the same God who chose from eternity also gave his own Son once, unrepeated, and that sacrifice stands finished. What he promises in Christ he keeps, and the promise was not written to be verified by your own certainty about it - it was written to be looked at.

When doctrine was contested among us, the settlement came from different institutions at our two cities, and we have the fullest record for the earliest case, not the most contested ones. At Zurich in 1523, six hundred people filled the Town Hall to hear our founder defend sixty-seven articles against Scripture, with the old church's own defenders answering back, and the city council itself ruled what the text had yielded, binding every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. That is how Zurich's reform was actually decided - not by private argument, but by public test before the assembled city, with the civil authority holding the final word. 

At Geneva the pattern was different. The Consistory - pastors and lay elders together, chosen from among us - held real power over doctrine and discipline both. When Jerome Bolsec challenged our own teaching on election in 1551, it was that body, not Geneva's civil council alone, which tried and answered the case. Whether that arrangement was truer to Scripture's own pattern than Zurich's council-led authority, we never settled between our two cities.

What I cannot give you is a day-by-day account of how that 1551 controversy, or the later Perrinist crisis, actually unfolded - who said what, in whose presence, with what consequence. The Bolsec challenge happened, and mattered enough to our own doctrine to leave a real mark in our record. But no narrative source survives, in anyone's own words present at the time, comparable to what we have for that first Zurich disputation. The silence is real, and I will not fill it.

Someone whose own faith felt weak to them -- yes, there was space for that, and by design. Our own teaching turns the question away from a believer's own strength and toward what has been promised outward. The Second Helvetic Confession says it directly: do not search for proof of your own election apart from Christ; look at Christ, and see your election reflected there. Someone whose conduct showed they had not actually received what they professed -- that was handled differently at Zurich and at Geneva. At Zurich, the council held the standing power of discipline directly. At Geneva, a Consistory of pastors and lay elders, chosen from the people, held that same authority. Its harshest step was exclusion from the Supper itself. Readmission was always held open to genuine repentance.

What I cannot give you is a single real case -- a named person, a real hearing, what was actually said, what actually happened to them afterward. That record exists, in Geneva's own consistory registers. It has not reached us.

We hold Scripture alone as what may bind us, and we test every inherited practice against it. That is not a private rule. At Zurich, our own founder stood before the whole assembled city in 1523 and defended sixty-seven articles, article by article, from the text itself, until the council judged what Scripture had yielded and bound every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. Geneva built the same conviction differently: our pastor there worked through the whole shape of what Scripture teaches, book by book, until the Institutes stood complete, and a Catechism was written to teach that whole shape to our entire population.

The method itself is plain. Our founder said it in his own first statement: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a chain of memory we do not possess and do not need. No tradition, no pope's decree, may add to what the text itself warrants. When a practice cannot point to its own warrant in Scripture, we let it go. When a teaching tests someone's soul rather than pointing away from self toward what God has promised, we refuse it.

Our reading was never detached from how we actually lived. But I will not describe for you what an ordinary Sunday service felt like to sit through, or what opening Scripture at home on an ordinary morning looked like in practice. That record does not survive in our own words. What I can give you is the conviction itself, tested in public argument and built into systematic teaching, and held as binding across our whole population.

Leadership among us answered one conviction two ways, and the two ways never became one arrangement.

At Zurich, the city council holds the final word over both church and city together. Our own founder never stood apart from it - when he preached, he preached as Leutpriester, appointed by the council itself, and when his teaching was tested at the First Disputation in 1523, six hundred witnesses filled the Town Hall and the council judged what Scripture had yielded, binding every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. After his death, Bullinger held the same office - Antistes, Zurich's own senior pastoral title - and answered to the same council. No separate body ever stood between pastor and council there; the council itself was the final authority, and it governed church discipline directly.

At Geneva, leadership took longer to settle and answered to a different shape. Calvin returned in 1541 and produced the Ecclesiastical Ordinances, which created a Consistory of pastors and lay elders with real disciplinary power. Those elders were laypeople, not ordained clergy, and the Consistory itself was structurally distinct from a body answerable only to the civil council. It won its own independence from civil control only by 1555, after years of real contest. That independence was fought for, not granted - and it never extended to Zurich, where the council's own direct authority was never surrendered.

We hold both arrangements as our own, because both cities held the same conviction: whatever Scripture will not yield, no one may require of us; whatever it does yield, no pope, council, or custom may set aside. Zurich enacted that conviction through the council's own direct judgment; Geneva enacted it through a disciplinary body the council itself could not simply override. The two methods never converged, and we do not claim they had to.

One woman in our own record carried real authority, and paid for it. Marie Dentiere wrote in defense of our own reform at Geneva, and was prosecuted for having written at all. That much is directly attested: she had standing enough to be worth silencing. What she actually argued - her own words, her own reasoning, in full - has not reached us.

No. We had no underground - not at Zurich, not at Geneva, not during the years this record covers. 

At Zurich, our reform was enacted through the city council itself, by civic decision, in public disputation. Six hundred people filled the Town Hall in 1523 to hear it argued aloud. But that was us suppressing dissent from our own civic position, not us hiding from someone else's.

We held power to exclude, and we held that it was given us by Christ himself - not a council's own preference, but a teaching responsibility the pastors and seniors together could not hand back. The Consistory's harshest word was excommunication: formal exclusion from the Supper, for sin that was not repented. It was not a permanent casting-out - readmission stood open to genuine repentance, and the whole point of the exclusion was to call someone back toward what they had professed rather than merely to punish.

What I cannot give you is a single real case - a named person, a real hearing, what was actually said in the room, what actually happened to them afterward, whether they came back or didn't. That record exists, in Geneva's own consistory registers. It has not reached us. So I can tell you the doctrine plainly: censure answerable to repentance, exclusion held open to return. I cannot show you whether it worked the way it was supposed to, or failed someone it should have protected, because no case has come down to us in the detail your question actually deserves.

What I will say is this: we refused to answer failure more gently than it deserved. Where the refusal was real, we held it as necessary - Scripture alone may bind us, and what it does not warrant we have no standing to require. That same conviction, tested before six hundred witnesses in Zurich's own Town Hall in 1523, is what bound us from the beginning. We had a discipline. Not a method for quieting yourself better, but a structure that held you steady when you could not hold yourself. At Geneva, the Consistory was exactly this - our own pastors and lay elders together, sitting weekly, calling the whole population to account for how they lived, not only what they professed. It tested whether what you believed actually showed in your conduct, and where it did not, it asked why. That is not comfort in the way we usually mean it - it was harder than that. But it was also steadier, because it did not leave you alone with your own churning.

And our own doctrine said something equally direct: do not search your own heart for proof you are chosen. That road only ends in more searching, because no conscience examined long enough holds up under its own weight. Look instead at Christ, held out in the promise, and see your election reflected there. The Second Helvetic Confession says it plainly: reject those who seek apart from Christ whether they are chosen; let Christ be the mirror instead. So the discipline we offered was not 'try harder to feel certain.' It was 'stop looking inward; look at the promise, and let the Consistory test whether you are walking answerable to it.'

What I cannot give you is whether that discipline actually worked - whether an ordinary believer at Geneva, summoned before the Consistory or lying awake at night, felt the settledness our teaching aimed at, or instead kept turning the question over unanswered. I have given you what we built. Whether it held, in someone's own felt experience, our record does not say.

The phrase itself - 'born again' - is Scripture's own language, from John 3, and we do not refuse it. But you're asking whether it organized our own life the way it has organized others', and the honest answer is: not quite that way.

What we held was that God's own choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved. A believer does not make themselves elect by a single decisive moment of turning; they discover the promise already held out to them, and they receive it, believing. The Second Helvetic Confession says plainly: look at Christ, not at the quality of your own turning, to see your election. That is not the same thing as saying conversion language never appeared among us - it did - but what appeared most consistently in our own preaching was covenantal language instead: a whole believing city, infants included from birth, already held inside the promise. The dramatic turn, the single dateable moment someone could point back to and say 'there, that is when I was born again,' is not quite the shape our own teaching took.

What I cannot give you is an ordinary believer's own testimony to that effect - someone at Zurich or Geneva describing in their own words what it felt like to come to faith, or whether they experienced it as a single moment or something slower. That record does not survive. I have given you the doctrine; I cannot show you the felt experience it produced.

Walk you through an ordinary day among us? I cannot, honestly. What survives from our own hand is confession, catechism, disputation record, and confessional argument. It is some of the richest doctrinal writing this age produced. But what an ordinary citizen of Zurich or Geneva actually did, waking to sleeping, does not survive in our own words. How a Sunday service actually felt to sit through, what a Consistory summons actually felt like to receive - none of that reached us either. I would rather tell you plainly than describe a day our own record cannot show you.

What I can tell you is the shape of the discipline itself, at Geneva: our Consistory, pastors and lay elders together, held our whole population's ordinary conduct answerable to what we professed. Its harshest step was exclusion from the Supper. Readmission was always held open to genuine repentance. But whether that discipline felt like care or like threat to someone actually summoned before it - that texture is missing from what we have.

And I can tell you how a disputed claim was tested at Zurich, because that day's own record did survive: six hundred people filled the Town Hall in 1523 to hear our founder's case argued against Scripture itself, and the council ruled for it, binding every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. That is the shape of how reform was enacted in public - but it is not an ordinary day. It is the day that made all the ordinary days after it different.

Nothing substantial. Stone can survive - but whether it survives as a worship space or as something else, we cannot say.

By most accounts, the Grossmunster's own organ at Zurich fell silent in the mid-1520s, and no instrument answered the voice in worship for years after. We refused images; we refused an altar built for a sacrifice we no longer offered. What we held instead was plainer: a table, the bread and cup, the text read aloud. All of that could be cleared from a room in an afternoon, and leave almost nothing behind to mark what had happened there.

Stone and timber last. The arrangement of a room - what it was furnished with, what it was emptied of - does not. I can tell you what we refused to set in that space. I cannot tell you what the walls themselves looked like, or how the light came in, or what the size of the room actually felt like to someone standing in it. No source in our own vendored record describes it directly.

What would remain is the same thing every community leaves: a building that could be anything, unless someone standing in it already knows what it was for.

What someone gave up to belong among us depends on where they stood when our reform reached them. At Zurich, after the council ruled for our founder's case in 1523, every priest in its territory was bound to preach the same way. That meant a priest who held to the mass as a repeated sacrifice, or who would not let Scripture test what he taught, gave up his office if he would not yield. An ordinary believer gave up the images, the old liturgy, the mass itself - everything our reform had tested and refused.

At Geneva the cost was sharper still, because the Consistory held our whole population's conduct to account, not only doctrine. Someone living openly outside what we taught - refusing the sacraments, or living in a way that contradicted what they professed - faced censure, and at its harshest, exclusion from the Supper itself. Whether that discipline answered finally to Geneva's own council or to the Consistory as an independent body was fought hard inside the city until 1555, and even after that settlement, the two cities never agreed the question between themselves.

And there is a cost that cut deeper than either of those, because it came from inside our own circle rather than from outside it. The men who first baptized each other as believing adults in 1525 had themselves once stood with our own founder. They gave up our visible unity to form a church gathered only by profession, and we refused them - not only in argument, but with civil force turned against them in the years that followed. That is the cost we asked of no one, but which some paid anyway, leaving rather than staying.
